items.summary: At AI Engineer New York, Anthropic drew on lessons from Unix and Linux to explain how agents can tackle bigger projects without overwhelming developers.

sourceMetadata.pageDescription: At AI Engineer New York, Anthropic drew on lessons from Unix and Linux to explain how agents can tackle bigger projects without overwhelming developers. The AI Engineer New York 2026 conference kicked off this morning with a series of workshops, including Anthropic discussing how to orchestrate its Claude Managed Agents. Of particular interest was a brand new feature, announced on Friday, called dynamic workflows — or simply “flows,” as the presenters repeatedly called it. Flows are defined as “a new type of multiagent orchestration, built for your most ambitious workloads.” CJ Avilla and Harrison Stall, both Members of Technical Staff at Anthropic, began by invoking some operating system projects of the past — from Ken Thompson building the original Unix operating system, through to Linux evolving from one person (Linus Torvalds) to layers of trusted maintainers. The lesson: agents need the same level of organization in order to do the types of big, ambitious projects Anthropic envisions for dynamic workflows.

sourceMetadata.author: @dair_ai
sourceMetadata.pageDescription: 🥇Top AI Papers of the Week An agent is defined by its model and its harness, the program that organizes model calls, tool use, and information flow. Researchers at CMU train a proposer model to revise the harness based on execution feedback, while the solver model’s weights never change. Agents that search large document collections usually see the corpus as a flat set of files, so a relevant document gives no hint of how it connects to others. Researchers from Microsoft and colleagues introduce CorpusMap, a navigation layer built around the entities that recur across a collection. A common practice with long-horizon agents is to sample several rollouts and trust the answers they agree on. Researchers at Google show that agreement can hide shared errors, while disagreement often points to the correct alternative, and they built VeriHarness to verify rollouts with the same base model.
